newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Australian Grain-Harvest optimism, steady mkt.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Australian Grain-Harvest optimism, steady mkt.

text.p: The Australian grain market steadied last week as the big harvest began to roll in and as optimism returned to the trade.
Futures and Australian Wheat Board (AWB) indicative prices held modest gains while cash market prices were mostly steady.
"Very busy, a lot is happening," said Peter Howard of New England Agricultural Traders. "There's a slightly friendlier feel about it, we may have bottomed," he said.
Not all brokers agree that futures prices have reached their final floor, with big crops from Argentina, Australia and Canada hitting or about to hit the world market.
But the feeling is widespread that the next AWB pool announcement on Monday afternoon will show steady prices.
Howard and Guy Allen of GrainCorp both tip a steady price.

"I think the market is calling it to be mostly steady. If they raise it, I think it'll be bullish, if they lower it by A$5.00 I don't think it will have any effect. But I look for it to be mostly steady," Allen said.
The trade sees more good news in new-crop quality.

GrainCorp has received more than 800,000 tonnes of grain since the start of the harvest in New South Wales (NSW) which has returned this year to its status as Australia's biggest wheat-producing state for the first time in years. Fine weather produced receivals last week of 400,000 tonnes.

"The quality of grain received to date has been very good, though not as high as last year when 62 percent of grain was high protein," GrainCorp said in a statement Friday to mark first receivals from an eight million tonne NSW harvest.
Howard also told Reuters that crop downgrading fears because of rain had proven unfounded.
Protein started low but turned around and was improving as harvest progressed. "Quality excellent," he said.

With the harvest a little late but rolling on, AWB on Friday told Reuters that Australia was headed for exports from the 21.0 million crop of 17.0 million tonnes. GrainCorp expects NSW alone to export more than five million tonnes.

Wheat cash prices held in the past week, with Australian Standard White (ASW), in what Howard described as "some quite reasonable trades", sold into Newcastle at A$155.00 to A$160.00 a tonne for nearby delivery.
While not representing an increase in price, "there's a big difference between immediate delivery and further out," he said.
GrainCorp's Allen also saw cash prices steady over the week, with ASW delivered Newcastle on about A$146.00.
Over the past week, AWB indicator prices for ASW in the main centres were steady (Melbourne and Newcastle) to up by A$5.00 or A$6.00 a tonne (Adelaide and Fremantle respectively).

A steady upward trend in futures prices on the Sydney Futures Exchange saw market leader January 1997 rise to A$149.50 on Friday from A$147.50 on Monday. Volume was down to 169 futures trades for the week, less than the week before when a
trading damburst on the A$15.00 AWB pool price cut produced a record 261 trades in one day.

Australian markets took last week's USDA crop report in their stride. Most analysts saw the report as mildly bullish on the reduction in carryover stocks, others saw it as mildly bearish on the overall production estimates.
But the markets gained.
